## Isaiah 16: verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Moab is told to start paying tribute to Jerusalem again, which means submitting to God. Moab's king Mesha once paid Israel a tribute of lambs but stopped when Ahab died (2 Kings 3:4–5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-16/
- **Who gets the tribute:** the king of Judah, as the true "ruler of the land," because the northern kingdom was close to collapse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
- **"Sela":**
  - It could be the city later called Petra, or just the rocky country of Edom and Moab. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
  - Pulpit thinks it more likely means Moab's own rocky hideouts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
- **The route:** invaders blocked the northern crossings, so the tribute had to go the southern way, through the desert past the Dead Sea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
- Ellicott adds that the verse might also be calling Edom to submit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
- **Text note:** the Hebrew has one ram, and NET reads it as a plural ("rams") because a letter was probably dropped in copying. Pulpit says the word can mean a group of lambs. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm

**v. 2**
- Moab under judgment is confused, weak and exposed, like a bird thrown out of its nest. Its only hope is to submit to Jerusalem and its king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-16/
- **"Daughters of Moab":**
  - Ellicott: either the women driven from their homes, or the whole population. They flutter at the Arnon fords, unsure whether to go home or cross into a foreign land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
  - Pulpit: the people as a whole. It also reads the scene more hopefully: once the tribute is paid, the scattered people gather at the fords ready to cross back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm

**v. 3: Who is speaking? Commentators disagree.**
- **Ellicott:** Moab asks Judah's rulers for shelter, shade "black as night" under a blazing sun (compare Isa 32:2). He notes Kay's minority view that the prophet is telling Moab to protect fugitives from Judah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
- **Pulpit:** most critics hear Moabites, or a Moabite envoy in Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
- **NET:** the speaker is unclear. Perhaps the prophet plays a panicked Moabite refugee pleading with Judah's leaders (the commands are plural). Shade stands for shelter, and noon heat for Moab's suffering. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print
- **Guzik:** Isaiah urges Judah to hide Moab's refugees, probably out of sympathy because Moab is linked to David's family. He applies this to the church: it should shelter people who humbly flee to it under judgment, and never betray them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-16/

**v. 4**
- **"My outcasts" or "Moab's outcasts"?**
  - Pulpit: moving one accent mark gives "let the outcasts of Moab dwell with you." That reading has the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation), the Syriac, Lowth, Gesenius, Ewald and Cheyne behind it. Delitzsch and Kay keep the KJV's "mine outcasts." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
  - Ellicott prefers "outcasts of Moab," a renewed appeal to Judah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
  - NET translates "Moabite fugitives." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print
  - Bible Hub's own study note has God urging Judah to welcome Moabite refugees. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/16-4.htm
- **Guzik, an end-times reading:** following the NKJV, he sees a sudden switch, with Moab now asked to shelter Judah's outcasts. He cites Bultema, who reads vv. 4–5 as end-times prophecy: Jews flee the Antichrist and find refuge in places like Moab (Rev 12). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-16/
- **"The extortioner is at an end":**
  - Pulpit: this is the reason to give shelter, since it won't be for long. The extortioner is probably Assyria, which demanded heavy tribute. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
  - NET: the verbs describe the oppressor's end as if it had already happened. The opening word could mean "certainly," "for," or "when"; the last links it to v. 5. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print

**v. 5**
- **Ellicott:** "a throne" (not "the throne"). Isaiah has in mind the ideal king of chapters 9 and 11, whom he expected after Assyria fell. Hezekiah was only a partial picture of him. Compare Amos 9:11, "tabernacle of David." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
- **Pulpit:** a vision of the Messiah comes to the prophet when he sees the oppressor vanish. He doesn't know whether it will come soon or late. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
- **Guzik:** the Messiah's throne set up in the end times, and his wonderful reign. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-16/
- **NET:** a trustworthy king from David's family. "Hastening righteousness" may mean "skilled or experienced in" justice rather than "quick." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print

**v. 6**
- **Moab refused the offer:**
  - Pulpit: a new section starts here. Pride kept Moab from submitting to David's house, so its pride is what gets condemned. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
  - Ellicott: Moab's typical sin darkens the prophet's hopes. He says the Moabite Inscription (Mesha's stone) shows that pride, and Jeremiah 48:29 echoes this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
- **"His lies shall not be so":** better "his boasts are worthless." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm. NET says a word often translated "wrath" here means boastful outbursts. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print
- **Guzik:** this is the only place the chapters spell out Moab's sin. A small nation can be as proud as an empire, so look for pride in "small things." He cites Bultema: pride that humility doesn't break will be broken by justice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-16/

**v. 7**
- **"Moab for Moab":** the whole nation wailing over its fall, or the survivors wailing for the dead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
- **"Foundations" (KJV) or "raisin cakes":**
  - Pulpit: elsewhere the word always means raisin cakes ("flagons"), and that fits the following verses about lost crops. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
  - Ellicott: possibly a product Kir-hareseth traded in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
  - NET: the cakes could have a religious meaning (Hos 3:1), but here they stand for fine food that is now gone. Some read the word as "men." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print
- **Kir-hareseth:** probably the same as Kir-Moab (15:1). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm

**v. 8**
- **"Lords of the nations… broken down its choice plants":**
  - Pulpit: probably the Assyrians, who wrecked enemy fruit trees. It rejects Cheyne's reading that the strong wine "broke down," meaning made drunk, the lords. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
  - Ellicott: notes that most recent critics prefer the wine-made-them-drunk reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
  - Bible Hub's preview of the Geneva Study Bible names the Assyrians and other enemies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/16-8.htm
- **How far the vines reached:** north to Jazer, east into the desert, and across the Dead Sea (perhaps to En-gedi). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
- **Gill** (from a short preview): the fields wither from drought, from the enemy trampling and foraging, or because no one was left to farm them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/16-8.htm

**vv. 9–10**
- **Isaiah grieves:**
  - Guzik: Isaiah takes no pleasure in a rival nation's judgment. He compares Jesus weeping over Jerusalem (Matt 23:37–39). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-16/
  - Pulpit: tears "as genuine as Jazer's own" (quoting Kay). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
- **The "shout" in v. 9:**
  - Ellicott and Pulpit: the enemy's war cry, replacing the grape-treaders' song. Ellicott notes the same Hebrew word is used for both. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
  - NET agrees but allows that it could be harvesters' joy falling silent. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print
- **"I have made the shouting cease" (v. 10):** God speaks here.
  - Ellicott: the destruction is done by human hands but is God's righteous punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
  - Pulpit: the prophet's voice slips and reveals God behind him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
  - NET: the Lord appears to be the speaker. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print
- **Background:** "plentiful field" translates *Carmel*, meaning orchard or garden land. Pulpit describes winepresses (two vats cut in rock) and the custom of singing while treading grapes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm

**v. 11**
- **Who is grieving?** It could be the prophet or God; Ellicott thinks the prophet is more natural, though Isa 63:15 uses the phrase of God. The "bowels" were the seat of feeling and vibrate like harp strings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
- **NET:** the harp might suggest the sound of sighing, or sighing that repeats like strumming. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print

**v. 12**
- **Ellicott:** Moab's prayers to Chemosh at the high places are useless, like the prophets of Baal in 1 Kings 18. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
- **Pulpit:** pagans thought they would be heard for their many words (Matt 6:7) and wore themselves out. It cites Mesha's inscription mentioning high places. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
- **Guzik:** the pain of watching people in disaster turn to the wrong places for help. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-16/

**v. 13**
- **"Since that time" / "earlier":** an earlier word, now repeated.
  - Ellicott: Isaiah may be reusing an older prophet's oracle, or one he had been given earlier. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
  - Pulpit: it existed before, but the text doesn't say how long. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
  - Guzik: most of chapters 15–16 was given earlier, and the three-year deadline was added later. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-16/

**v. 14**
- **"As a hired worker counts the years":** counted exactly, neither more nor less than the contract. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm; https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=16&mode=print
- **How it was fulfilled:**
  - Ellicott: history doesn't record it, but Assyrian armies under Shalmaneser or Sargon probably invaded. Moab's "remnant," unlike Israel's, would not grow strong again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/16.htm
  - Pulpit estimates Moab's population (about 300,000) and says Moab put up little resistance to Ashurbanipal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/16.htm
  - Guzik: the date can't be checked independently. He cites Wolf on Sargon's campaign of 715 BC. He draws three lessons: a warning inviting Moab to repent, a lesson in how God judges the proud, and an assurance that God deals with other nations as he dealt with Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-16/

## Where readings differ (only what I could document)
- **The main split is over vv. 4–5.**
  - Ellicott and Pulpit read it as a historical scene (Moab asks Judah for refuge) that opens into a Messianic hope, with no fixed date.
  - Guzik, drawing on Bultema, reads it as end-times prophecy: Israel sheltering from the Antichrist, then Christ's reign.
  - (Links under v. 4 and v. 5.)
- **The speaker in vv. 3–4 is disputed:** Moab speaking to Judah (most), the prophet speaking to Moab (Kay), or Isaiah speaking to Judah (Guzik).
- I couldn't fetch Baptist, Methodist, Reformed, Lutheran or Pentecostal denominational sources, so I can't say how each tradition reads the chapter.
